Notes: Wormald: A small MS containing only laws, written around 1100 mainly by one scribe and owned (probably also made) at St Paul's, London; Wormald thinks it perhaps the earliest of the three large law collections of the early twelfth century. The main scribe's Old English is so faulty that Wormald suspects it was not his usual language, yet correctors and later rubricators worked to make the text usable; he links its interest in relations between English and Danes to the post-conquest regime and to Bishop Maurice of London. Wormald: Liebermann dated the main hand c. 1125–30, whereas Wormald puts it at the turn of the eleventh and twelfth centuries (s. xi/xii); he also notes that corrections Liebermann called sixteenth-century are medieval, and that the Talbot note Liebermann took as proof of continued St Paul's ownership in the sixteenth century proves nothing (pp. 165, 233, 230 n. 268, 234 n. 285).

English Translation: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 265
Notes: Wormald: Corpus 265 is a mid-eleventh-century Worcester compendium of canon law, penitential and liturgical texts for a working bishop, whose first part is among the most systematic surviving forms of the canon collection associated with Archbishop Wulfstan. Its separate second section contains IV Edgar, uniquely in both Latin and Old English, set between formulae for excommunicating and absolving enemies of the Church and the Maundy Thursday rite for reconciling penitents — a placing Wormald explains by the code's insistence on tithe. The Latin version, he suggests, was made so that a royal code could take its place in a learned Latin collection of church law, and a related twelfth-century collection (Barlow 37) hints that IV Edgar may have belonged to the collection from an early stage.

Wormald mentions it only as a parallel to the vernacular half of Corpus 190: it contains the second of the Old English letters Ælfric wrote for Wulfstan, and it is one of only two other MSS to combine the two Old English penitentials ascribed to Ecgberht, there joined with the Directions for a Confessor, which helps point that material to Worcester.

York, Minster Library, Add. 1 (York Gospels)
Notes: Wormald: A late tenth-century Gospel-book, perhaps completed at Canterbury and at York from Wulfstan's time onward, to which were added York estate records, three law-like Wulfstan tracts glossed by the archbishop, and, written by the scribe of the tracts, the sole surviving text of Cnut's 1019×20 letter to the English. Because the copying took place before Wulfstan's death in May 1023, the letter is uniquely close to its issue. The laying out of letter and tracts alike as clauses shows how little Wulfstan distinguished law from homily, and its placing in a holy book shows royal law being enshrined beside God's. Wormald: Liebermann dated the gospel book c. 1025 and the homilies and letter c. 1030–70; Wormald shows the MS is of the late tenth century and that the tracts and the letter were copied before Wulfstan's death in May 1023, since his hand glosses them (pp. 195, 197).
